verses.1:
Al-Mizan describes the chapter as a predominantly warning and fear-inspiring reminder. Its stories end in the ruin of tyrants and rejecters of God’s communications; its proofs compel recognition of divine unity and response to truth; and it portrays the Hour, resurrection, sinners’ terror, and the losers’ loss. It opens by consoling the Prophet: the Qur’an was not revealed to burden him with forcing people to answer his call. His duty is only to convey it. Revelation reminds people of God and His signs, hoping to awaken their fear so that they believe and become god-fearing; if they refuse, punishment or return to their Lord bearing their sins awaits them, and their tyranny cannot frustrate God. The context indicates that the chapter is Meccan. Reports calling (20:130) or (20:131) Medinite are not supported by their wording.

Ṭā Hā consists of the alphabetical letters with which some chapters begin, like Alif Lām Mīm and Alif Lām Rāʾ; their full matter lies beyond exegetical discussion, though reported explanations are considered among the narrations. Shaqāwah, unsuccessfulness, is the opposite of saʾādah, happiness, and, like happiness, includes worldly and otherworldly forms. Shaqāʾ may also mean taʾab, tiredness, though every shaqāwah is tiredness and not every tiredness is shaqāwah. Thus the revelation did not come so that the Prophet should exhaust himself making people accept it as part of his mission.

Tadhkirah is a reminder that restores what has been forgotten. Human fiṭra instinctively apprehends God’s existence, unity, necessary existence, divinity and Lordship, as well as religion, prophethood, resurrection, and judgment. Attachment to earthly life and its adornments makes hearts turn away from these implanted truths; this is metaphorically called forgetting because both states produce inattention. The reminder arouses fear of the consequences of action, thereby stirring the soul to turn wholly to truth until remembrance enables adherence to it. “Him who fears” therefore denotes those with apprehensive hearts receptive to truth: when reminded, fear is awakened and they believe. On one view, illā tadhkirah is a discontinuous exception: the Qur’an was not revealed to weary the Prophet, but as a reminder for one disposed to fear, remember, believe, and guard against evil. The verse itself suggests that tadhkirah functions as the object of “We have not revealed,” while tanzīlan in the following verse describes it: the Qur’an is a divine word sent down to remind the fearful.

The Creator of the earth and the high Heavens is specified as the One who sends down revelation because sending down requires an elevated source and a lower destination. The intervening creation is not mentioned here, since the point is revelation’s origin and destination, not the comprehensive ownership expressed elsewhere. ʿUlā means “high.”

The verses from (20:5) to (20:8) establish the unity and absoluteness of divine Lordship, the central point of the call and reminder. Al-istiwāʾ ʿalā ʿal-ʿarsh is an allusion to taking possession and holding the reins of regulation, not bodily sitting. God’s authority embraces creation: He owns all things and regulates their affairs, great and small. Lordship means precisely ownership and regulation, which explains why istiwāʾ is followed by statements of His all-encompassing ownership and knowledge. Al-Raḥmān is especially fitting here because raḥmah denotes effusion through bringing into being and regulating, and its intensive form conveys the multiplicity appropriate to this comprehensive regulation. Grammatically, al-Raḥmān is the subject and istawāʾ its predicate, with ʿalā ʿal-ʿarsh dependent on istawāʾ. The contrary parsing—making “The Beneficent is on the Throne” a complete clause and treating istawāʾ as a verb whose subject is what is in the heavens—is clearly incorrect.

“His is what is in the Heavens and what is in the earth and what is between them two and what is beneath the ground (al-tharā)” affirms His ownership of all that is known or perceptible and all that is not. Tharā may mean moist earth or earth generally, and what is beneath it is what lies in the earth rather than on its surface. Ownership of the constituents of heaven and earth entails ownership of heaven and earth themselves. This explains one pillar of Lordship, ownership, while regulation is its other pillar.

The progression from audible speech to al-sirr, what one keeps within oneself, and to akhfā, what is still more hidden, establishes God’s all-encompassing knowledge. Akhfā is a comparative or superlative of concealment, not a past verb meaning that God hides His knowledge. Whether one speaks what is in one’s mind, keeps it secret, or conceals it even to the point that one does not oneself know it, God knows it. The construction tersely answers an implied question about audible speech: if He knows the secret and what is more hidden, then He certainly knows what is uttered aloud. An interpretation that makes the secret concealed speech and the more hidden what merely passes through the mind is sound concerning secrecy, but speech is properly called sirr when suppressed within oneself; the broader explanation is preferable. Knowledge of all that occurs in His dominion entails His permission, will, and regulation of its ordered system. Thus this verse confirms the comprehensiveness of regulation just as the preceding verse confirms ownership; together they prove absolute Lordship.

The final verse may be read as the culmination of the preceding description—this One is God, and there is no god but He—or, more likely, as an independent and comprehensive assertion in which “God” is the subject, “there is no god but He” the predicate, and “His are the very best names” a second predicate. “There is no god but He” follows from His being the sole absolute Lord: an object of worship must own and regulate its worshipper, for worship expresses servitude and need. Since no Lord exists apart from Him, no true object of worship exists apart from Him.

The same conclusion follows from His best names. Worship is motivated by hope for a worshipped being’s good, fear of being forsaken or harmed, or recognition that it is intrinsically worthy of subordination. God owns every source of good; whatever others possess is bestowed by Him, while He remains its absolute owner and has power over those to whom He grants power. His names therefore encompass the sources of hoped-for good: He is the Bestower, Granter of Favor, Quickener, Healer, Provider, Of-Forgiving, Merciful, Rich, and Self-Sufficient. He alone is also the irresistible Dominator, strong Avenger, and severe in punishment, so He alone is worshipped in fear of wrath. Finally, only perfection merits worship: souls are drawn to beauty and minds submit before majesty. Every grace is a sign of His beauty and every splendor a sign of His majesty; hence no god or object of worship exists besides Him.

The best names are names bearing wholly beautiful adjectival meanings, such as Everliving, Omniscient, and Omnipotent, rather than mere proper nouns that only identify an essence. Naming can also mean describing, as in Say: Give them a name (13:33). Names may be unpleasing, such as oppressor or ignorant, or beautiful, such as just and knowledgeable. Even beautiful names differ: some contain only partial perfection and remain marked by deficiency and contingency, whereas names such as al-Ḥayy, al-ʿAlīm, and al-Qādir signify unalloyed perfection, abstracted from matter and composition. The latter are the best names and are fitting for God. The plural with the definite article in Lahu al-asmāʾ al-ḥusnā makes every such name His, and placing the predicate first makes this exclusive: any perfection found in others is His gift and disposition. This ownership extends even to names and attributes identical with His Essence, such as life, knowledge, and power.

verses.3:
Al-Mizan explains tadhkirah as a reminder that restores what has been forgotten. Human fiṭra instinctively knows God’s existence, unity, necessary existence, divinity and Lordship, together with religion, prophethood, resurrection, and judgment. Yet attachment to earthly life and its adornments makes people turn from these inherent truths; this is figuratively called forgetting because both turning away and forgetting result in inattention.

The reminder counters such heedlessness and the pursuit of worldly desire by arousing fear of the consequences of action. Fear activates the soul to devote itself to truth, so that remembrance returns and enables one to adhere to it. “Him who fears” thus means those whose apprehensive hearts are receptive to truth: when the reminder reaches them, their fear is aroused and they believe.

According to one view, illā tadhkirah is a discontinuous exception: the Qur’an was not revealed to make the Prophet weary, but to remind one disposed to fear, so that he remembers, believes in God, and guards against evil. The verse suggests that tadhkirah functions substantivally as the object of “We have not revealed”; tanzīlan in the next verse similarly functions as an object and describes this reminder, the Qur’an. Its meaning is that the Qur’an was not sent down to exhaust the Prophet, but to remind the fearful of the divine word sent down from God’s Presence.
verses.4: Al-Mizan explains that ʿUlā, “high,” is the plural of ʿulyā, the feminine of aʿlā. The Creator of the earth and high Heavens is identified as the sender of revelation because “sending down” (tanzīl) is appropriate only where revelation proceeds from an elevated origin to a lower destination. The earth and heavens are singled out not to enumerate all that exists, but solely to clarify that origin and destination; mentioning what lies between them would serve the different purpose of proving God’s all-encompassing ownership.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan holds that (20:5) begins the four verses establishing the unity of Lordship, which is the core of the summons and reminder. Al-istiwāʾ ʿalā ʿal-ʿarsh is an allusion to taking possession and assuming the reins of regulation, not to bodily sitting. In a manner befitting His grandeur and holiness, God’s authority dominates creation: He owns all things and regulates all their affairs, whether great or small. He is the one Lord, and Lordship means ownership together with regulation. This explains why His istawāʾ ʿalā ʿal-ʿarsh is followed by reference to His all-encompassing ownership and knowledge.

Al-Raḥmān is especially apt because raḥmah signifies effusion through bringing things into being and regulating them; its intensive form conveys the multiplicity appropriate to this universal regulation. Grammatically, al-Raḥmān is the subject and istawāʾ its predicate, while ʿalā ʿal-ʿarsh depends on istawāʾ. The commentary rejects the proposed parsing in which “The Beneficent is on the Throne” forms the subject and predicate, followed by a verb istawāʾ whose subject is what is in the heavens. Things conform to His will and command, but that is not the grammar or meaning of this verse.
verses.6: Al-Mizan explains al-tharā as moist earth, or earth generally, and “what is beneath the ground” as what lies within the earth rather than on its surface. God’s ownership therefore encompasses everything in the heavens, on and within the earth, and between them—what human senses know, such as people, animals, and plants, as well as what remains unknown and imperceptible. Since a material thing is nothing other than its constituent parts, ownership of everything in the heavens and earth also entails ownership of the heavens and earth themselves. The verse thus establishes ownership, one of the two pillars of Lordship (rubūbīyyah), whose full meaning is ownership and regulation.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains al-jahr bi al-qawl as audible, raised speech, opposed to al-Isrār. Al-sirr is speech kept within oneself, while akhfā is a comparative or superlative meaning “more hidden,” as the verse’s progression from uttered speech to secret and then to what is still more hidden shows. The commentary rejects the claim that akhfā is a past verb meaning that God knows the secret and hides His knowledge.

The verse confirms God’s all-encompassing knowledge: whether one manifests what is in one’s mind, conceals it within oneself, or keeps it hidden even to the point that one does not oneself know it, God knows it. Its concise construction answers an implicit question about audible speech: He certainly knows it, since He knows the secret and what is more hidden. One exegete’s distinction between speech hidden from others and thoughts passing through the mind is valid concerning secrecy, but speech is properly called sirr when suppressed in oneself; the commentary therefore prefers the wider explanation.

God’s knowledge of all that occurs in His dominion entails His pleasure, permission, will, and regulation (tadbīr) of the ordered system. Thus the verse confirms the comprehensiveness of His regulation, just as the preceding verse confirms His comprehensive ownership. Together, ownership and regulation constitute absolute Lordship.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan considers the verse either the culmination of the preceding description—this One already described is God—or, more likely, an independent and comprehensive statement: “God” is the subject, “there is no god but He” its predicate, and “His are the very best names” a second predicate. The declaration that there is no god but Him follows either from the preceding proof that He alone is the absolute Lord or from the explanation of His best names that follows.

Ilāh means an object of worship, or the true object of worship. Worship is an expression of servitude, ownership, and need, so the worshipped being must own and regulate the worshipper’s affairs—that is, be his Lord. Since God alone is Lord of everything, He alone is the true object of worship.

Worship may arise from hope for a worshipped being’s good, fear of the harm resulting from its abandonment, or recognition that it is worthy of submission. God owns every source of good; others own only what He gives them, while He remains the absolute owner of what He has made them own and has power over those to whom He grants power. His best names include the sources of all hoped-for good: He is the Bestower, Granter of Favor, Quickener, Healer, Provider, Of-Forgiving, Merciful, Rich, and Self-Sufficient. He alone therefore deserves worship in hope of His good. He is also the irresistible Dominator, strong Avenger, and severe in punishment; no aggression occurs without His permission. He therefore deserves worship in fear of His wrath, even if one is not humbled by His greatness.

God alone is intrinsically worthy of worship because perfection alone merits submission from deficiency. The soul is attracted to beauty, and the mind and heart submit before majesty; all grace belongs to Him, every existent thing is a sign of His beauty, and every splendor a sign of His majesty. Thus there is no god or object of worship besides Him because His are the very best names.

The best names are names that signify beautiful adjectival meanings, such as Everliving, Omniscient, and Omnipotent, rather than proper nouns whose function is merely to indicate an essence. Describing may itself be called naming, as in Say: Give them a name (13:33). Names are either unpleasing, such as oppressor, tyrant, and ignorant, or beautiful, such as just and knowledgeable. Beautiful names in turn include those containing some perfection but still mixed with deficiency and contingency, and those signifying unalloyed perfection, free of matter, composition, deficiency, and flaw. Names such as al-Ḥayy, al-ʿAlīm, and al-Qādir belong to the latter class and are the names most fittingly applied to God.

Every best name is His: the plural with the definite article in Lahu al-asmāʾ al-ḥusnā denotes universality, and the preceding predicate indicates exclusivity. He owns these names for Himself; whatever corresponding perfection appears in another belongs to that person only through His dispensation. This ownership may also be affirmed of attributes identical with His Essence, including life, knowledge, and power.
verses.9: Al-Mizan explains that the question introduces and confirms the commencement of Moses’ story.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains makth as remaining or tarrying; inās as a strong seeing or sensing of something familiar; qabas as a firebrand; and hudā as either guidance or a source through which guidance is attained.

The context indicates that Moses was travelling with his family from Midian to Egypt, near the Valley of Ṭuwā on Mount Sinai, on a dark winter night after losing the way. Seeing a fire, he intended to go to it: if someone was there, he would seek directions; otherwise, he would bring back a burning brand to warm them. His command to his family to stop suggests that others were also present, while the emphatic “surely I see” indicates that Moses alone saw the fire. The wording also implies, “Stop so that I may go to it,” in hopes of bringing a firebrand or finding a guide.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan explains that Ṭuwā is the valley on Mount Sinai which God called sacred. Moses was ordered to remove his shoes out of reverence for it, since its holiness arose from its becoming a realm of divine nearness, presence, and communion. Sacred places and times are honored because of their connection with an auspicious event, rite, or act of worship made part of the Shariah; apart from such a connection, no place or time is inherently superior to another.

When Moses heard, “Surely I am your Lord,” he knew immediately and without theoretical inference or proof that it was his Lord speaking. This is the nature of revelation: in direct divine speech the recipient does not suppose another speaker or another source for the words. If such certainty depended on acquired reasoning, it would not be reception of unseen knowledge without an intermediary.

Other verses confirm a veil or messenger in the communication, but this does not contradict its being revelation from God. Revelation, like God’s other acts, is not devoid of intermediaries; what matters is whether the recipient attends to the intermediary or to God. If he attends to the intermediary, it is a message conveyed through it; if he attends to God, it is revelation from Him even where an unnoticed intermediary exists. The following command, “so listen to what is revealed,” confirms this description.

The address “Surely I am your Lord” thus teaches Moses that he stands in divine presence and has been singled out for special attention. It differs from “I am God” or “the Lord of the Worlds”; the later declaration, “Surely I am God,” is not repetition, since it excludes any other participant from the revelation while forming part of the revelation’s content. Finally, leaving unnamed the one who called conveys the sudden and surprising character of the sign for Moses.

verses.13:
Al-Mizan explains ikhtiyār as selecting what is better among alternatives for the sake of a purpose. God’s choosing of Moses was therefore for the divine purpose of giving him Prophethood and the Message: in divine knowledge he was the most qualified to bear them.

In context, “And I have chosen you” is not merely indicative information but an imperative act by which Moses is appointed Prophet and Messenger. “So listen to what is revealed” consequently commands him to attend to the revelation constituting that Prophethood and Message.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan holds that these verses set out the prophetic side of Moses’ revelation, while the ensuing discourse concerning the staff and Pharaoh begins the Messengership. The three verses on Prophethood contain religion’s pillars: belief in God’s unity and the Resurrection, while Prophethood is not separately stated because the Prophet himself is being addressed; and action, comprehensively summarized by “therefore serve Me.”

“Surely I am God” is the self-disclosure of the One called God: the present speaker is known directly, whereas the divine Name identifies Him for the hearer. From “there is no god but I” follows “therefore serve Me,” since the One from whom all things begin, by whom they subsist, and to whom they return is alone truly worthy of worship.

Prayer is singled out after the general command to worship because it most fully represents servitude and realizes remembrance of God. The most immediate interpretation of li-dhikrī is “keep up prayer to attain My remembrance”: the lām is explanatory and dhikr is annexed to its object. Other readings make the phrase dependent on prayer or worship, take the lām temporally as praying when God or the prayer is remembered, understand dhikr as oral, inward, or both inward and outward remembrance, or take the annexation as God’s remembrance of the worshipper. Some also restrict prayer to remembrance alone or to sincere remembrance without showing off, though the wording itself does not establish every such restriction. Other explanations exist, but the first is the interpretation most readily indicated by the context.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains the coming Hour as the ground of the command to worship. Although worship follows necessarily from divine unity, legislation, commands, and prohibitions would be futile without a day on which people are recompensed, the obedient distinguished from the disobedient, and the good from the evil. The Hour is therefore an unavoidable decree.

“I am about to make it manifest” apparently means that God almost conceals the Hour and gives no information about it, so that it arrives unexpectedly and suddenly. Alternatively, its concealment distinguishes those who worship God sincerely for His sake from those motivated by hope of reward or fear of punishment. It is also claimed, on the authority of an oral tradition, that the expression means, “I almost hid it from Myself,” an emphatic idiom for extreme concealment. The coming of the Hour is so that every soul may be rewarded according to its striving.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan explains that both pronouns refer to the Hour: one must not be turned away from believing in it and remembering its decisive significance, since every soul will be recompensed for its striving. Ṣadd means turning away, and radā means perishing.

Following low desire explains disbelief in the Hour: such desires lead a person to deny it and then abandon service to the Lord. Conversely, belief in the Hour is the truth that saves from perishing. The past tense in “follows his low desires,” despite its conjunction with a present-tense expression, may suggest that following desire causes disbelief.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan regards this question as the beginning of the revelation of Moses’ Messengership, after the revelation concerning Prophethood has concluded. It is a confirmatory question about his staff, intended to make Moses describe its inanimate character and properties so that its transformation into a serpent would have its full effect on him.

The feminine demonstrative tilka most likely refers to a feminine noun such as a stick, piece of wood, or the staff itself, rather than to the masculine al-shayʾ, “thing.” Since it was already obvious that the object was a staff, the question was not seeking its name or essence, but its qualities and uses. Moses’ detailed answer accordingly reflects a rhetorical practice in which an evident object is questioned in order to elicit its description.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan explains that Moses identifies the staff, says that he leans on it, and uses it to beat leaves down for his sheep; maʾārib means further needs or uses dependent on it as a means.

It is said that Moses’ extended description reflects the pleasure of conversing confidentially with the Beloved, beginning with “my staff” to evoke its general benefits. But it is not needless verbosity, since he summarizes its remaining functions in “I have other uses for it,” and the preceding question itself called for an account of its characteristics.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains that, when Moses cast down his staff, the inanimate object unexpectedly became a swiftly moving serpent. Elsewhere it is called a thuʿbān, a mighty serpent. The command to take it without fear and the promise to restore its former state show that Moses feared the moving serpent.

This fear is khawf: the beginning of precautions to avoid evil. It is distinct from khashyah, an agitation of the heart incompatible with the perfection of courage. Khawf is permissible for prophets, whereas khashyah is reserved for God alone.

verses.36: Al-Mizan explains that God’s words grant all of Moses’ petitions. Like “And I have chosen you,” the statement is an imperative enactment, not merely information.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan explains that God recalls a favor bestowed on Moses at the beginning of his life, before his selection for Prophethood and the Message. A soothsayer had told Pharaoh that an Israelite child would end his kingdom, so Pharaoh ordered the killing of Israelite sons. When Moses was born, God inspired his mother to nurse him and, if she feared Pharaoh’s agents, place him in a chest and cast it into the Nile. It would reach Pharaoh’s palace, where the childless Pharaoh would adopt rather than kill him, and Moses would be returned to his mother.

Moses’ sister watched the circumstances around the palace, found Pharaoh’s servants seeking a nurse, and directed them to her mother. His mother thus received her own child as nurse, and her eye was comforted. The shift to the majestic plural expresses divine grandeur: God thwarted Pharaoh’s attempt to extinguish His light by having Pharaoh raise his own enemy in his household.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan explains that the revelation to Moses’ mother was an inspiration cast into the heart while asleep or awake, not prophetic revelation. Such waḥy is not confined to prophets, whereas prophetic revelation is given to men and women do not become prophets.

The inspired instruction was to place Moses in a tābūt, a chest, and cast it into the yamm, the great river, identified here as the Nile. The first casting may mean placing him in the chest and the second casting him into the river. The river’s casting him upon the shore is phrased as an imperative to indicate an unavoidable generative decree. Pharaoh would take him up; he was God’s enemy through claiming divinity and Moses’ enemy through killing newborn sons.

The casting of “love from Me” is a further favor: all who saw Moses were drawn to love him, so Pharaoh would spare and treat him kindly until he was returned to his mother and her grief ended. “That you might be brought up before My eyes” expresses God’s special, watchful care and compassion; it may specifically include restoring him to his mother for upbringing. The shift from the majestic plural to the first-person singular suits this intimate discourse of care.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan explains that the revelation to Moses’ mother was an inspiration cast into the heart while asleep or awake, not prophetic revelation. Such waḥy is not confined to prophets, whereas prophetic revelation is given to men and women do not become prophets.

The inspired instruction was to place Moses in a tābūt, a chest, and cast it into the yamm, the great river, identified here as the Nile. The first casting may mean placing him in the chest and the second casting him into the river. The river’s casting him upon the shore is phrased as an imperative to indicate an unavoidable generative decree. Pharaoh would take him up; he was God’s enemy through claiming divinity and Moses’ enemy through killing newborn sons.

The casting of “love from Me” is a further favor: all who saw Moses were drawn to love him, so Pharaoh would spare and treat him kindly until he was returned to his mother and her grief ended. “That you might be brought up before My eyes” expresses God’s special, watchful care and compassion; it may specifically include restoring him to his mother for upbringing. The shift from the majestic plural to the first-person singular suits this intimate discourse of care.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan connects Moses’ sister’s offer to direct Pharaoh’s servants to a suitable nurse with the preceding divine care: Moses was restored to his mother so that she would rejoice rather than grieve. The return to the majestic plural in “So We brought you back” continues the earlier plural discourse rather than constituting a rhetorical shift.

The verse then recalls further favors: Moses killed the Egyptian, feared execution by Pharaoh’s council, and was delivered by leaving for Midian. There he tended Jethro’s flocks, married Prophet Jethro’s daughter, and remained among the people of Midian for years. “We tried you with a severe trying” means that God tested him repeatedly. Fitnah originally denotes assaying gold in fire to separate the good from the bad, and is used for punishment or testing through hardship and ease, though it commonly denotes hardship.

Al-Mizan considers qadar in “you came hither as ordained” most fittingly to mean miqdār, the measure of knowledge and deeds, or actual perfection, which Moses acquired through those successive trials, escape, and residence in Midian. The trials can be called favors because they purified him like gold in fire, or because of the reward consequent upon them. The interpretation that fitnah refers only to hardship after his departure, based on the consequential fāʾ, is not decisive, since such consequence need not indicate temporal sequence. Likewise, qadar as measure is preferable to interpreting it solely as a prior decree. The final naming of Moses further honors him.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan explains iṣṭināʿ as beneficence so complete that the recipient becomes ascribed to the benefactor. Thus God’s choosing Moses “for Myself” means making him pure for Himself: all that he possesses is God’s favor, without another having a share in him. Even if iṣṭināʿ is taken simply as favor, it implicitly conveys purification, which is among the greatest divine bounties to Moses.

Interpretations that make the phrase mean appointment as God’s authority, choice for revelation and the Message, or choice for divine love add qualifications not found in the verse. Against the objection that this choosing is disconnected from the preceding list of favors by the address “O Moses,” Al-Mizan holds that the address may itself be an additional honor, preparing an intimate shift from the majestic plural to the singular: “And I have chosen you for Myself.”
verses.42:
Al-Mizan explains that this restates the earlier command to Moses to go to Pharaoh, now addressing Aaron as well in fulfillment of Moses’ petition that he be associated in the mission.

The plural “My signs,” though only two had then been shown, promises further divine signs and support whenever needed; it should not be reduced to a plural used merely for two. “Be not remiss in remembering Me” prohibits heedlessness, and dhikr here most suitably means calling people to believe in God alone, rather than inward or oral remembrance alone.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan explains that Moses and Aaron are jointly commanded to go to Pharaoh and to speak gently, not harshly or sternly; this is a central etiquette of propagation. The discourse may quote a further address to both messengers, as suggested by their ensuing joint response.

“Haply he may mind or fear” expresses the prospect that Pharaoh may heed the reminder, accept what proof requires, believe, or at least draw near to acceptance and comply with some requests. Fear is a precursor to such acceptance. Laʿalla does not mean that Pharaoh’s repentance or salvation was inevitable. In divine speech, ʿasā and laʿalla retain the sense of hope as understood from the situation, although God Himself is not ignorant or expectant as human speakers are.

Al-Mizan rejects al-Rāzī’s claim that the reason for sending Moses to one known not to believe can only be accepted without explanation. A command concerns an act in relation to its agent, who is an incomplete cause and can choose to obey or disobey; Pharaoh’s response was therefore possible in that respect, even though it was impossible when all the factors of his complete cause are considered together. This is the position of those who uphold free choice. Determinism instead makes duties generally problematic, and its proposed answer reduces imposition of duty to an apparent one for completing proof and removing excuse.

The mission was not vain even if Pharaoh would not believe. A true invitation perfects some toward prosperity and completes others in their wretchedness. Without the latter possibility, there would be no test, the case would not be complete, and excuses would not be eliminated.

verses.45:
Al-Mizan explains yafruṭa ʿalaynā as Pharaoh’s hastening to punish them before the invitation and miracle are completed, while yaṭghā means that he might exceed all bounds in tyranny, intensify the Israelites’ suffering, and become still more audacious toward God.

Their fear does not conflict with the prior assurance that Pharaoh could not reach them. There, Moses feared for himself because of his earlier killing; here their fear concerns the propagation of the mission. It is also possible that the verse combines two fears: Moses’ earlier fear when he fled and Aaron’s fear after learning of his Messengership. The reported dialogue need not have occurred in a single sitting.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan explains “Fear not” as assurance against Pharaoh’s tyranny. “Surely I am with you both: I do hear and see” means that God is present with them, hears what is said, sees what is done, and will not forsake them. It is therefore a metonymy for divine guarding and help, not merely a statement of universal knowledge or presence.

The commentary rejects the argument that hearing and seeing must be attributes additional to knowledge because otherwise the wording would repeat itself. Divine presence and witnessing differ from knowledge, and decisive proofs establish that the Essential Attributes—Everliving, All-Powerful, All-Knowing, All-Hearing, and All-Seeing—are alike and collectively identical with the Essence. Fundamental beliefs require certain proof, so a linguistic presumption against repetition cannot establish such a doctrine.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan explains that, after assuring Moses and Aaron of protection and help, God renews the command to go to Pharaoh and specifies their message. They must announce that they are the two messengers of Pharaoh’s Lord, call him to faith and the remaining articles of belief, demand that he release the children of Israel with them, and forbid him to torment them. The command is repeated at each changed stage of the dialogue: first to Moses, then to Moses with Aaron after the petition, and finally after their fear has been answered.

Their claim to have brought a sign from Pharaoh’s Lord confirms their message by proof. The indefinite āyah leaves its number unstated and conveys the sign’s greatness, status, and clarity. Releasing the Israelites and ceasing their torment are secondary obligations laid upon Pharaoh.

“Peace is on him who follows the guidance” concludes the message as a valedictory greeting and summarizes the invitation: peace and happiness belong to one who follows guidance, in this world and the Hereafter, without encountering what he dislikes.
verses.48:
Al-Mizan explains that the warning clarifies why peace is assigned only to those who follow guidance: chastisement, its opposite, comes upon whoever rejects God’s signs or the true call and turns away.

The wording of the two verses also disdains Pharaoh’s pretended greatness and worldly arrogance. Faʾtiyāhu conveys direct approach more strongly than a simple command to go to him, while “say” omits “to him” as though he were insignificant. The repeated words “your Lord” strike Pharaoh, who claimed supreme lordship, with the fact that he has a Lord. Peace and punishment are then stated generally of whoever follows or rejects, rather than directly addressing Pharaoh.

This is nevertheless wholly consistent with the prior instruction to speak gently. It is truthful speech without flattery, timidity, intimidation, or harshness before Pharaoh’s false authority and vanity.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan introduces this section as the account of Moses and Aaron’s mission to Pharaoh: their demand that the Israelites be released, the display of the signs, the contest with the magicians and their submission, followed by Israel’s night journey, the sea’s division, Pharaoh’s pursuit, and the drowning of his army.

On Pharaoh’s question, “And who is your Lord, O Moses?”, the commentary says that the preceding summons is omitted because Pharaoh’s reply implies it. Pharaoh addressed Moses as the principal messenger, though Aaron was his associate, and asked about “your Lord” because he feigned indifference to the assertion that God was his own Lord. In the idolatrous outlook described here, the transcendent Creator was considered too exalted to be directly worshipped or approached. Worship, sacrifice, and intercession were instead directed to favored creatures—angels, jinn, holy persons, and sometimes deified kings—who were called gods and lords. Thus Pharaoh was not denying a Creator or even denying that he had gods; he pretended that Moses and Aaron were inviting him to adopt one god among others. He was himself a deified king who worshipped idols while being worshipped by his people. Al-Mizan consequently rejects explanations that make Pharaoh a mere obstinate believer in God, a materialist, a philosopher, a star-worshipper, or an adherent of other proposed doctrines: none accords with the fundamental creed of idolatry as explained.

Moses’ answer, “Our Lord is He Who gave to everything its creation, then guided it (to its goal),” identifies creation as the particular existence given to every thing and hidāyah as its being directed to the end for which it was created. Every being has faculties, properties, and causes fitted to lead it toward its perfection, as an embryo is equipped for its eventual human completion. The use of thumma indicates that a thing’s movement toward its end is subsequent in rank to its existence. This is universal guidance, not merely the special guidance of human beings: every thing is furnished with what connects and moves it toward its goal. The ordered relations and movements within each thing and throughout the universe are both divine guidance and divine regulation (tadbīr); because regulation belongs to the One who brings things into being, all existence and its attributes subsist through Him. The verse therefore proves that He alone is Lord, owning and directing all things. It is a more eloquent answer than simply calling Him “the Lord of the Worlds,” because it both asserts universal lordship and supplies its proof. Guidance is particularly mentioned because the context is one of calling and guidance. Al-Mizan rejects interpretations that make khalqahu mean a spouse, make the verse mean that creatures received every blessing, or make hidāyah merely evidence for God’s existence and oneness; these readings are remote from the context and impose unwarranted restrictions on the wording.

Pharaoh’s question about the former generations turns from lordship to resurrection. Moses’ description of universal guidance entails prophecy, reckoning, reward, and punishment; idolatrous deniers of resurrection therefore object by asking how extinct peoples, whose persons and deeds seem lost through death and time, can be recompensed. Moses answers that their complete knowledge is with his Lord in a Book. This unrestricted knowledge misses neither persons nor acts, remains with God, and is preserved in a magnificent comprehensive record without change, loss, or erasure. “My Lord errs not, nor does He forget” negates ignorance after knowledge: error would confuse one known thing with another, and forgetfulness would remove it from knowledge. Thus God can judge past generations despite the disappearance of their traces. Absolute lordship itself proves such knowledge, for the Lord owns, sustains, and directs every being; nothing can be absent from Him. Moses says “my Lord,” rather than “our Lord,” because here he himself is describing the Lord’s knowledge of the former generations. Al-Mizan rejects the view that Pharaoh merely sought historical information in order to distract Moses from his message.

The making of the earth an expanse, paths upon it, rain from the cloud, and varied plants for humans and cattle continues the account of universal guidance. Earthly life, its paths and provisions, are a stage in which humanity takes provision for its higher life and journeys toward proximity to God. Rain and vegetation display guidance throughout the causal order: the sky rains, water descends, plants grow, and humans and animals are directed to their sustenance. Azwājan may mean similar kinds and species of plants, or their male and female pairing. The shift to “We have brought forth” rhetorically suits the extraordinary production of diverse life from one source, water. These are signs for those possessed of nuhā, minds that restrain caprice. “From it We created you and into it We shall send you back and from it will We raise you a second time” gives the complete human course: creation from earth, return to it, and resurrection from it for return to God.

“All of” the signs shown to Pharaoh apparently includes the staff, the hand, and the other signs shown during Moses’ mission until Pharaoh’s drowning; likewise, Pharaoh’s rejection and refusal covers the whole period, not merely its beginning. Pharaoh’s charge that Moses came with magic to expel the Egyptians from their land both evades the truth of the signs and politically incites the people by portraying Moses as an enemy of their homes and homeland. His challenge proposes a fixed appointment for a matching display of magic in a central or level open place. Moses chooses the festival day, in the bright forenoon and before a public gathering, so that the outcome will be visible to all. Pharaoh then departs, assembles his magicians and other agents of deception, and returns.

Moses warns Pharaoh, the magicians, and the rest of Pharaoh’s party not to forge a lie against God, lest a severe punishment annihilate them. Although their accusations of magic and political plotting are lies, the forgery against God apparently means the idolatrous attribution of divinity, intercession, and worldly regulation to partners beside Him. Forgery is a form of lying based on false causes, and falsehood cannot yield a true or enduring result; hence everyone who forges such lies fails to attain the desired end.

Moses’ warning produces disagreement among them, apparently beginning among the magicians; some may have hesitated to confront him. Pharaoh and his aides conceal this dispute and replace Moses’ clear warning with the claim that Moses and Aaron are two magicians plotting to expel the people and abolish their best tradition. That tradition is the long-established idolatrous order, centered upon Pharaoh’s divinity, which they treat as sacred because their communal identity, power, and life depend on it, not because it is true. They urge the magicians to gather all their artifice, discard division, stand in ranks, and overcome Moses, using every inducement and threat, including promises of favor and nearness to Pharaoh.

At the contest, the magicians offer Moses the choice of casting first or letting them do so. He tells them to cast, relying on his Lord’s promise. Their ropes and rods appear, through magic, to run like snakes; the illusion is seen by Moses and the spectators alike. Moses then conceives a light, inward, momentary fear, not one expressed in his conduct. The impressive magic makes it seem close to his sign. Al-Mizan rejects the suggestions that he feared people would confuse the miracle with magic, or that they would disperse before he cast his staff: those explanations conflict with God’s earlier assurance of victory, the sequence of the verses, and Moses’ willingness to let them cast first. Their enchantment was mighty in appearance, but it was illusion, whereas Moses’ sign was real.

God reassures Moses: “Fear not, surely you shall be the uppermost,” and commands him to cast what is in his right hand. The staff becomes a serpent and devours what the magicians made. Calling it merely “what is in your right hand” indicates that things possess no independent reality: by God’s will it is a staff, and by His will it is a serpent. The contest thus contrasts God’s absolute power, to which the realities and names of things are subject, with a human contrivance that has no reality. The miracle visibly establishes Moses’ superiority; the declaration that magicians do not succeed establishes it in truth. Magic produces only spectators’ fantasy and cannot yield real happiness or success. Moses’ staff and the magicians’ sorcery are accordingly a parable of truth’s eventual destruction of every falsehood, however much falsehood adorns itself to resemble truth.

When the staff devours their work, the magicians are “cast down” in prostration, a passive wording that portrays their humiliation by divine power and the irresistible victory of truth. Their declaration, “We believe in the Lord of Aaron and Moses,” testifies both to God’s lordship and to the messengership of Moses and Aaron. Pharaoh responds by threatening to cut off opposite hands and feet and crucify them on palm trunks. His accusation that Moses is their chief and teacher of magic is another political fabrication: he presents their faith as a prearranged conspiracy to drive out Egypt’s people, in order to turn the masses against them. The Qur’an does not state whether he carried out the threat.

The magicians’ reply shows the transformation worked by witnessing the truth. Pharaoh’s former splendor, authority, and worldly adornment are exposed as vain illusion. Having been overtaken by truth, they abandon fear, flattery, desire, and infatuation with worldly appearance; they will not prefer Pharaoh, with all he claims to possess, to the clear signs and to their Creator. Pharaoh, by contrast, sees only himself, imagines that hearts can believe only by his permission, and treats material existence and pleasure as the whole of human happiness. His threat presumes that killing and worldly punishment are final. The believers know that humanity has an everlasting life beyond this transient one, so worldly misery cannot harm one who attains eternal happiness, while worldly enjoyment cannot benefit one who meets eternal misery. Hence Pharaoh may decide only matters of this world’s life. The “clear arguments” apparently include the staff’s transformation, its devouring of the ropes and rods, and its return to its former state; the less likely alternative is that they saw one sign and inferred many others.

Their further declaration that they believe in their Lord so that He may forgive their sins and the magic to which Pharaoh compelled them indicates that they had been forced into magic, either when summoned from their homes or when compelled to enter the contest. They choose God’s forgiveness over Pharaoh’s favor because God is better without qualification and more abiding than everything else. Their references to God as “He Who made us,” “our Lord,” and “God” form a proof: as Creator, He is the source of every good; as Lord, He owns and directs them and is the proper object of faith and servitude; and as God, He possesses all perfection and is absolutely good.

Their appeal for forgiveness rests on the fact that whoever comes to his Lord guilty belongs in hell, where he neither dies to escape its suffering nor lives a pleasant life. Conversely, whoever comes as a believer with good deeds receives the high ranks—the Gardens of perpetuity beneath which rivers flow—as the reward of purification through true faith and pious deeds. This directly counters Pharaoh’s threats of enduring punishment and his promise to make them his near favorites.

Finally, God commands Moses to travel by night with the Israelites and make for them a dry path in the sea, without fear of being overtaken or afraid. Fa-ḍrib may refer to striking the sea with the staff so that a path is made, or to establishing such a path; yabas denotes a place whose water has gone. Pharaoh follows with his armies, and the indefinite repetition in “there came upon them of the sea that which came upon them” forcefully depicts the horror of their fate. “And Pharaoh led astray his people and he did not guide (them) aright” is not mere repetition: it refutes his claim that he led them only in the right way.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan explains Moses’ answer as a proof that God alone is Lord: He gives every thing its own particular existence, then directs it toward the end and perfection for which it was created. Hidāyah is universal guidance, not guidance restricted to humanity. Every being is equipped with the faculties, properties, and causal connections by which it moves toward its proper goal, as the embryo is equipped for human completion. Thumma indicates that this movement follows existence in rank.

The ordered relations, actions, and movements of individual things and of the whole universe manifest this guidance; viewed otherwise, they manifest divine regulation (tadbīr). Since the regulator is the One who brings things into being, every existence and attribute subsists through Him. His creation of all things establishes His ownership and direction of them, and therefore proves that there is no lord apart from Him.

This reply suits Pharaoh’s feigned question about “your Lord.” Rather than merely asserting, “Our Lord is the Lord of the Worlds,” Moses both declares universal lordship and gives its proof. The verse mentions guidance rather than regulation because the setting is one of propagation and guidance. Al-Mizan rejects readings that make khalqahu mean a matching spouse, make the verse mean that God gave creatures every blessing, or make hidāyah only the demonstration of God’s existence and oneness; these readings depart from the context and impose unwarranted limitations on the wording.
verses.51:
Al-Mizan explains that bāl, originally associated with a thought occurring to the mind, here means state. Pharaoh’s question about the former generations shifts from lordship, which Moses’ answer had settled, to resurrection. Universal human guidance requires prophecy and the reckoning, punishment, and reward by which obedience is distinguished from wrongdoing; idolaters deny this. Pharaoh skeptically asks what becomes of extinct peoples whose persons, deeds, and traces have disappeared: how could they be recompensed when they seem to be no more than stories?

Moses’ ensuing reply—that their knowledge is with his Lord in a Book—shows that Pharaoh regards resurrection as improbable because death and time seem to have removed all knowledge of them and their deeds. Moses answers by affirming God’s absolute and detailed knowledge of those former generations.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan says that God’s unrestricted knowledge encompasses every individual of the former generations and every one of their deeds. Its being “with my Lord” means that it neither departs nor disappears from Him, and its being “in a Book” confirms that it is recorded, preserved, and comprehensive, omitting neither small nor great. Thus the disappearance of former peoples and their traces creates no obstacle to their recompense.

“ My Lord errs not, nor does He forget” completes this answer. Apparently both clauses deny ignorance after knowledge: ḍalāl in relation to knowledge means confusing one known thing with another through a change in the object as known, while nisyān is the departure of something from knowledge after it was present. God neither confuses their identities, properties, and actions nor loses them through forgetfulness. His knowledge from the beginning is thereby affirmed, and He can reward or punish them accordingly.

Calling Him “my Lord” proves this knowledge, for a rabb owns and directs what belongs to him. God’s absolute lordship means that every being depends on Him and is present to Him through His regulation; to suppose anything unknown to Him would suppose it absent from Him, which is contradictory. Moses uses “my Lord,” not “our Lord,” because he himself is describing the Lord’s knowledge of the former generations, rather than answering a question about the Lord to whom he and Aaron call. Al-Mizan rejects the view that Pharaoh was merely asking about past history in order to divert Moses from his message.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan reads these verses as a continuation of the account of God’s universal guidance. God made the earth a place for humanity’s earthly life and for taking provision toward its higher heavenly life; He made paths for earthly needs that also recall the path to humanity’s ultimate goal, proximity to Him. He sends rain, the source of springs, rivers, and seas, and brings forth varied plants, thereby guiding humans and cattle to the food by which life continues.

The rain, its descent, vegetation, and nourishment show the causal order through which divine guidance operates. Azwājan may mean similar kinds and species of plants, or the pairing of male and female plants. The shift from the third person to “We have brought forth” rhetorically suits the extraordinary production of diverse forms of life from a single source, water. These are signs of God’s guidance and lordship for those endowed with nuhā: minds that restrain one from following caprice.

verses.55: Al-Mizan explains that “it” is the earth: humanity is created from it, returned to it at death and becomes part of it, then raised from it again to return to God. The verse thus presents humanity’s complete course of guidance.
verses.56: Al-Mizan holds that “Our signs, all of them” likely means the staff, the hand, and the other signs Moses showed Pharaoh throughout his mission before Pharaoh drowned, not necessarily signs displayed together at its beginning. Likewise, Pharaoh’s rejection and refusal encompass all his rejection and refusal during that period.
verses.57: Al-Mizan explains that Pharaoh calls Moses’ signs magic in order to avoid conceding their truth and the truth of Moses’ summons. He also accuses him of plotting to expel the Egyptians from Egypt, a political charge meant to distract and provoke the people by depicting Moses as an enemy who would drive them from their homes and homeland.
verses.58: Al-Mizan says that mawʾid apparently denotes an appointed time, while ikhlāf al-waʾd means failing to keep the appointment. Makān suwā may mean a central open place or a place level with its surroundings. Pharaoh’s meaning is: they will produce magic to match Moses’ in order to refute his proof and defeat his purpose, so he should fix an unbroken appointment between them at such a place.
verses.59: Al-Mizan explains that Moses fixes the contest for the festival day, apparently a feast when people adorned themselves and the markets, and for the early forenoon, when sunlight spreads. The public gathering is an operative condition of the appointment: what Moses and the magicians do is to occur visibly before the people, at a time of clear sight.
verses.60: Al-Mizan takes Pharaoh’s turning away to mean that he left the meeting where the appointment had been made in order to prepare. “Settled his plan” means that he assembled his scheme: the magicians and all other workers and means by which he intended to blind and confuse the people. He then came to the appointed contest.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan explains Moses’ “Woe to you” as a severe threat addressed to Pharaoh, his magicians, and the other members of his plot. The warning not to forge a lie against God apparently concerns idolatry itself: attributing divinity, intercession, and the regulation of the world to beings besides God. Pharaoh’s branding of the signs as magic and of the summons as a political plot are lies, but they do not by themselves constitute attributing something to God; nor does countering a miracle with acknowledged magic. The warning therefore chiefly concerns the fundamental falsehood of associating partners with Him.

The threatened, indefinite punishment is severe and annihilating. The declaration that whoever forges a lie fails is a universal principle: forgery is lying based on false causes, and false causes cannot produce true, enduring consequences or happiness. Its result is only loss and disappointment; in this respect the statement is broader than a warning restricted to those who forge lies specifically against God.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan explains that Moses’ warning against idolatrous forgery produces real disagreement among Pharaoh’s party, apparently beginning among the magicians. Some of them may have hesitated or even considered refusing to confront Moses. Pharaoh and his aides conceal the resulting discussion rather than publicize Moses’ clear warning and proof.

They instead revive Pharaoh’s accusation that Moses and Aaron are two magicians plotting to expel the Egyptians and abolish their “best traditions.” This tradition is the established idolatrous order by which Egypt was administered, with Pharaoh at the forefront as the people’s god. Though Moses’ argument had exposed its falsity, they present it as a sacred inherited national tradition on which their identity, power, greatness, and way of life depend. The threat of losing homes and possessions, together with the loss of this order, is used to incite the people.

They urge their supporters to gather all their artifice, suppress disagreement, come in united ranks, and overcome Moses. Pharaoh reinforces this appeal with both incentives and threats, including promises of reward and nearness. Thus their secret discourse is their attempt to remove the division awakened by Moses’ admonition and unite the magicians and the people against him.

The threat of losing homes and possessions, together with the loss of this order, is used to incite the people.

They urge their supporters to gather all their artifice, suppress disagreement, come in united ranks, and overcome Moses. Pharaoh reinforces this appeal with both incentives and threats, including promises of reward and nearness. Thus their secret discourse is their attempt to remove the division awakened by Moses’ admonition and unite the magicians and the people against him.
verses.65:
Al-Mizan explains that the magicians offer Moses the choice of casting first or allowing them to cast first. Moses tells them to cast, yielding the initiative while relying confidently on his Lord’s promise. Their ḥibāl, ropes, and ʿiṣiyy, rods, create the visual illusion of running serpents and snakes, like the appearance of Moses’ staff.

The compressed wording suggests that immediately after Moses’ command they cast and their illusion appeared. What Moses saw was also seen by the spectators: the magic deceived and frightened people’s eyes. The verse’s particular mention of Moses among those who saw it prepares for the account of the fear that briefly arose within him.

verses.67:
Al-Mizan explains that Moses’ fear was a light, inward, momentary feeling, as indicated by its indefiniteness and its confinement to his soul; it did not appear in his body or conduct. The impressive appearance of the magicians’ enchantment made him feel that it might seem equal or nearly equal to his sign, though their work was illusion and his was a real miracle.

The commentary rejects the view that he feared people would confuse magic with his miracle and fail to believe, since this conflicts with God’s assurance that Moses and his followers would prevail and with Moses’ trust in the divine command. It also rejects the view that he feared people would disperse before he cast his staff, because the verse links his fear to what appeared from their magic, he had allowed them to cast first, and God’s response promises superiority rather than preventing dispersal. Their magic was mighty in appearance, but God would remove all doubt by making the staff devour what they had conjured.
verses.68:
Al-Mizan explains God’s command, “Fear not, surely you shall be the uppermost,” as reassurance that Moses will surpass the magicians in every respect and that their magic cannot harm him. He is commanded to cast his staff, which will become a serpent and devour their magical work.

Calling the staff simply “what is in your right hand” alludes to the fact that a thing has no reality independent of God’s will: by His will it is a staff and by His will it becomes a serpent. The contest therefore contrasts God’s absolute power, to which the realities and names of things are subject, with human fashioning that is only futile artifice. The staff’s devouring of their work visibly manifests Moses’ superiority, while the explanation that their work is only a magician’s plan manifests its reality: their magic has no truth, whereas his sign is real.

The magician’s lack of success is a universal rule. Magic creates only a fantasy in spectators and cannot lead to true happiness. Falsehood may adorn itself to resemble truth, but truth ultimately effaces and devours it; Moses’ staff and the magicians’ sorcery therefore exemplify every truth that destroys an appearing falsehood.

verses.70:
Al-Mizan explains that the passive wording, “the magicians were cast down making obeisance,” portrays their humiliation by divine power and the triumph of truth over them, as though they had no choice but to fall in prostration. Their confession, “We believe in the Lord of Aaron and Moses,” is testimony both to God’s lordship and to the messengership of Moses and Aaron.

Pharaoh’s response is a threat for their faith. He promises to cut off their right hands and left feet and crucify them on palm trunks. His claim that Moses is their chief who taught them magic is a political accusation: he portrays their conversion as a prearranged conspiracy in which they feigned opposition to Moses, then deserted him so that the masses would follow them and Egypt’s established order would collapse. Pharaoh makes this allegation to incite the people against them, as he had earlier accused Moses of plotting to expel the population. The Qur’an does not state whether he carried out the threatened punishment.

verses.72:
Al-Mizan sees the magicians’ reply as evidence of the transformation produced by their witnessing the signs of truth. Pharaoh’s former splendor, authority, and worldly adornment had filled their hearts, but they are now exposed as false imaginations and a deceptive mirage. The believers are freed from cowardice, flattery, desire, and infatuation with worldly display; they attach themselves to truth, submit to God’s authority, seek only what He wills, and fear none but Him.

Pharaoh, by contrast, sees only himself and imagines that people can believe only with his permission. His claims to be lord of Egypt and master of its armies are empty, but he supposes reality follows his falsehood. His threats also show that he regards bodily, transient worldly life and its material pleasures as the whole of human reality and happiness.

The magicians will not prefer Pharaoh—with all the wealth, power, and pleasures he claims—to the clear arguments they have received and to their Creator. They see this as the choice between falsehood and truth, or mirage and reality. They know that human life is everlasting beyond this immediate world: worldly misery does not harm one who attains eternal happiness, and worldly enjoyment cannot help one who suffers eternal misery. Thus they do not fear losing this life, and tell Pharaoh that his decision reaches only the life of this world. The clear arguments apparently include the staff’s becoming a serpent, devouring the ropes and rods, and returning to its original condition; the alternative that they saw only one sign and inferred further signs is possible but unlikely.
verses.73:
Al-Mizan explains that the magicians’ plea for forgiveness includes both their sins generally and the magic to which Pharaoh compelled them. Their being compelled may refer either to their being summoned from their homes before Pharaoh or to being forced to enter the contest after their secret disagreement. Their faith expresses their choice of God, their Creator, over Pharaoh, in hope that God will forgive them.

“And God is better and more abiding” completes the reason for their choice: His forgiveness is better than Pharaoh’s favor and more enduring than anything else, so nothing is to be preferred to Him. It also counters Pharaoh’s claim to be more abiding in punishment. Their three descriptions of God form a proof: He is “He Who made us,” so every good derives from Him; He is “our Lord,” the proper object of belief and servitude because He owns and directs; and He is “God,” absolutely good because He possesses every perfection.
verses.74: Al-Mizan explains this as the magicians’ reason for believing in God and seeking forgiveness. One whose sins remain unforgiven comes to his Lord guilty, and the guilty person belongs in hell, where he neither dies to escape its punishment nor lives a pleasant life.
verses.75:
Al-Mizan explains that the high ranks are the ascending levels of the Gardens of perpetuity, granted to the one who purifies himself through true faith and pious deeds. This is the inevitable consequence of belief and good works, just as hell is the consequence of sin arising from disbelief or disobedience.

The verses answer Pharaoh’s threats and promises to the magicians. His severest worldly punishment is still death, which can end a criminal’s suffering, whereas the guilty in hell neither die nor enjoy life. His promise to make them among his near favorites is answered by the believers’ reception of the highest ranks and everlasting gardens beneath which rivers flow. God’s reward, not Pharaoh’s favor, is the real reward of purification.

verses.77:
Al-Mizan explains that isrāʾ is travel by night and that “My servants” are the Israelites. Moses is commanded to make a dry path in the sea for them. Fa-ḍrib may mean striking the sea with the staff so that a path results, or establishing a path; yabas denotes a place from which water has disappeared, and darak means being overtaken by a consequence.

The repeated, indefinite expression that the sea came upon Pharaoh’s army with what came upon them forcefully conveys the horror of their drowning. “And Pharaoh led astray his people and he did not guide (them) aright” is not a redundant repetition: it refutes Pharaoh’s own assertion that he led his people only by the right way.

verses.80: Al-Mizan explains that God recalls delivering the Israelites from Pharaoh, who was drowned, after their prolonged suffering. The covenant on the blessed side of the mountain may refer to Moses’ forty-night appointment for the revelation of the Torah. Here al-ayman, “the blessed,” is an accusative adjective of jānib, “side.”
verses.81:
Al-Mizan holds that “Eat” is a command expressing permission. Ṭayyibāt, “the good things,” describes the sustenance God gave; it cannot imply that sustenance attributed to God is divided into good and non-good. Being inordinate with these provisions means responding to them with ingratitude rather than thanks, as in the Israelites’ complaint that they could not bear one kind of food.

God’s wrath becoming “due” means that it becomes necessary, as a debt becomes due. Wrath is an active Divine Attribute: God wills an unpleasant affliction for the disobedient servant and prepares its causes. Fa qad hawā literally means “has fallen,” and is explained as perishing.
verses.82:
Al-Mizan describes the verse as a confirmed promise of mercy after the preceding threat. Tawbah is return, whether from disobedience to obedience or from polytheism to monotheism; likewise, belief may be belief in God or in His signs, messengers, and laws. Although the Israelites are addressed, forgiveness is not confined to one people. Thus, God is, though God knows best, most Forgiving toward every person who returns from polytheism or sin, believes in Him, His signs, or His laws, regrets what he has done, and replaces the disobedience in question with obedience.

Ihtidāʾ is the opposite of ḍalāl. The wording thumma, “then,” apparently first indicates constancy in the repentance itself: one must not return to the particular sin repented from. This is akin to the condition of amendment in: Except those who repent after that and amend, then surely God is Forgiving, Merciful (3:89; 24:5). Yet this alone raises two difficulties: why Ghaffār, the intensive form “most Forgiving,” is used for one sin followed by repentance, and why repentance and belief would be required when one may disobey a law out of desire while still acknowledging it.

The commentary therefore says that, where repentance and belief occur together, they may mean repentance from polytheism and belief in God. “Does good” then means obeying God’s commands and avoiding His prohibitions. God’s abundant forgiveness concerns repeated sins—mistake after mistake—of one who has repented from polytheism and complies with the laws; this accords with: If you shun the great sins which you are forbidden, We will do away with your small sins (4:31).

The verse adds a further condition: the believer who does good must reach this through its proper way and door. The Qur’an makes belief and good works effective only with belief in the Messenger in the sense of surrendering to him, obeying him in major and minor matters, learning religion from him, following his path without obstinacy or satanic innovation, and accepting his guardianship in religious and worldly affairs. God has made this obligatory, as in: The Prophet has a greater claim on the faithful than they have on themselves (33:6).

The Israelites’ recurrent hesitation concerning Moses and Aaron’s guardianship explains the placement of this condition after the warning against excess and wrath. Thus “then continues to follow the right direction” means being guided to the Messenger’s guardianship by following him in religion and worldly affairs. The commentary finds no proof for interpretations that detach ihtidāʾ from belief, good action, and this guardianship—such as mere lifelong adherence to belief, freedom from another’s doubt, adherence to the Prophet’s practice, knowledge of reward, cleansing the heart, or generally protecting belief from contradiction.
verses.83:
Al-Mizan understands these verses as the conversation at Moses’ mountain appointment, where the Torah was revealed. God asks why Moses preceded his people to the meeting; Moses answers that they were following his track and would soon catch up, while his own haste was to seek God’s pleasure.

It is likely that those following him were the seventy men chosen for the appointment, not all the Israelites, since Aaron had been left as deputy over the people. The question may have been put to Moses either upon his arrival or at the end of his stay; if at the latter time, it naturally leads into God’s following disclosure that the people had been tried. This assumes, in accordance with the narrations, that the trial occurred after they considered Moses’ absence prolonged, without requiring forced exegetical explanations.

verses.85:
Al-Mizan explains fitnah as trial and test. The Samaritan is said to have led the people astray because, by molding and producing the calf for worship, he was one contributing cause of their error. The fāʾ in “So surely We have tried your people” is explanatory: Moses’ statement that they followed his track suggested that those left behind were well, and God corrects this assumption by disclosing that they had been tried and had gone astray.

The explicit phrase “your people,” rather than a pronoun, may distinguish all Moses’ tribe here from the approximately seventy men who were with him in the preceding verses.
verses.86:
Al-Mizan explains that Moses returned fiercely angry and sorrowful. The people’s breach of their promise meant that they had failed to act as his proper successors during his absence, as supported by: Evil is it that you have done after me (7:150).

The “goodly promise” may mean either the Torah and its law, whose acceptance brings happiness in this world and the Hereafter, or God’s promise to deliver them from their enemy, establish them in the land, and grant them great blessings. “Did then the time seem long to you?” refers to the interval of Moses’ absence, until they despaired of his return and their unity dissolved. Their worship of the calf was excess in unbelief after belief, bringing God’s displeasure and constituting their failure to take Moses’ place properly. Other explanations are possible: that they failed to follow Moses to the appointment, or that they disobeyed his order to obey Aaron until his return.
verses.87:
Al-Mizan explains bi-malkinā as the people’s claim that they did not break Moses’ promise while controlling their own affair. It may also mean that they did not use their own property to fashion the calf, and therefore had not deliberately set themselves on it: they merely carried the people’s jewelry, threw it down, and the Samaritan took it, cast it into fire, and produced the calf.

Awzār means burdens or weights, and zīnah means jewelry such as necklaces, earrings, and bracelets; the jewelry may have belonged to Pharaoh’s people. Qadhf, ilqāʾ, and nabdh all mean casting or throwing. The Samaritan either cast into the fire what they had cast down, or cast what he possessed just as they cast what they had been made to carry, and then brought forth the calf.
verses.88:
Al-Mizan takes “he brought forth” to indicate that the Samaritan made the calf secretly and then surprised the people by displaying it. A jasad is a body or corpse without spirit; therefore the calf had neither soul nor life, while khuwār means a calf’s sound.

“And thus did the Samaritan cast. So he brought forth for them a calf” may be independent Divine speech, with the people’s quotation ending at “then we cast them”; in that case, “they said” refers to some people and “for them” to others. “But he forgot” may refer either to Moses—whom they claimed had forgotten his god and gone to seek it on the mountain—or to the Samaritan, who forgot his Lord after knowing and believing in Him. Since “This is your god and the god of Moses” is plural in attribution, the apparent sense is that others assisted the Samaritan.
verses.89: Al-Mizan says that the verse reproaches the Israelites for worshiping a calf that could not answer one who called upon it, repel harm, or bring benefit. Reason itself shows that a lord must answer one seeking protection or benefit and must govern the harm and benefit of its servant, marbūb.
verses.90: Al-Mizan says this further censures the Israelites and exposes the gravity of their sin. They ignored not only the evident judgment of their intellects and perception, but also Aaron’s explicit warning. Their Prophet told them that the calf was only a test, that their true Lord was the Beneficent, and that they were required to follow Aaron and obey his command.
verses.91:
Al-Mizan explains that the worshipers would not abandon the calf until Moses returned, so that they could see what he said and commanded regarding it.

Moses then reproached Aaron, his appointed deputy, whom he had instructed: Take my place among my people, and act well and do not follow the way of the mischief-makers (7:142). “What prevented you?” means, in effect, what made Aaron fail to follow Moses’ way by stopping their error. Moses’ severity was for God’s sake: he asks whether Aaron disobeyed the order to follow him and not the way of the mischief-makers.
