verses.94:
Al-Mizan explains Yā bna umm, “O son of my mother,” as an appeal to mercy intended to calm Moses’ anger. Moses had seized Aaron by his beard and head in order to punish him.

Aaron’s apology is that forcefully stopping calf worship at that stage would have divided the Israelites: only some would obey, leaving obedient believers and disobedient polytheists as opposing groups. Their apparent unity would have become discord, perhaps even killing. Since Moses had ordered Aaron to act well, Aaron feared that Moses would accuse him of causing this division rather than awaiting his decision. Moses accepted his excuse, forgave him, and prayed for both of them: He said: My Lord! Forgive me and my brother and cause us to enter into Thy mercy, and Thou art the most Merciful of the merciful ones (7:151).
verses.95: Al-Mizan explains that, after addressing Aaron, Moses turned to the Samaritan, one of the three parties involved in the test and the one who led the people astray. Khaṭb means a grave matter that concerns a person; Moses asks what was the serious affair the Samaritan had undertaken.
verses.96:
Al-Mizan notes that baṣar can denote both the physical organ of sight and perceptive insight of the heart, though baṣīrah is seldom used for the organ. It discusses competing grammatical analyses of qabḍah, “a handful,” without finding the objection to its feminine ending decisive. Athar is what remains as evidence of something, including a footprint; rasūl denotes one who carries a message and may refer to a human messenger, Gabriel, or other messenger-angels.

The Samaritan’s statement answers Moses’ question about both the nature of his deed and its motive. “I saw what they did not see; so I took a handful from the footprints of the messenger, then I threw it” indicates the deed, while “thus did my soul commend to me” states that his soul impelled him. The Qur’anic context itself does not clarify the statement fully, which explains the exegetical disagreement.

Most scholars, following certain oral traditions, say that the Samaritan saw Gabriel—either descending to Moses or riding before Pharaoh’s forces at the sea—took dust from his footprint or his horse’s hoof, and later threw it upon the fashioned calf. Those reports assign the dust the power to give life, so that the calf moved and lowed. Al-Mizan rejects this explanation because it contradicts the Book’s explicit designation of the calf as a jasad: a jasad is a body without spirit or life and cannot describe a living body.

Abu Muslim is reported to offer another explanation: the “Messenger” is Moses, whose athar is his sunnah and whose rasm is what he commanded and followed. On this reading, the Samaritan claims that he perceived the people’s belief to be false, took some of Moses’ religion, and cast it aside; calling Moses “the Messenger” in the third person would be mockery, and the calf’s lowing would have been artificial. The commentary objects that the verse’s sequence makes the casting follow the taking of the handful, which follows seeing, whereas this reading reverses the required relation. It also makes the Samaritan neither a monotheist nor an idolater, though Moses’ following words identify the calf as the Samaritan’s god; and addressing Moses in the third person is unlikely.

A further conceivable interpretation identifies the Messenger’s athar with Egyptian gold jewelry, allegedly belonging or attributed to Moses. The Samaritan would then claim superior knowledge of goldsmithing and statuary, cast the jewelry into fire, and produce a hollow calf whose lowing arose from air passing through it. But this too leaves unresolved the third-person reference to Moses, the designation of the jewelry as the Messenger’s athar, and the description of the Samaritan’s worshiped calf as an enticement of his soul.
verses.97:
Al-Mizan explains this as Moses’ punishment of the Samaritan after his sin was established. “Begone” sentences him to exclusion from society: neither he nor anyone else was to touch the other, and he was cut off from exchange, shelter, companionship, speech, and the other forms of human association. “Touch (me) not” therefore means that he was condemned to enduring loneliness and isolation throughout his life.

It is claimed that this was Moses’ supplication, producing an incurable disease that made others feverish when they approached, or that he suffered devilish insinuation and fled from people crying, “Touch (me) not.” The latter would be a good explanation if its tradition were authentic. The unfailed threat apparently foretells a God-decreed punishment at a specified time in the Hereafter, though it is also possible that it is a supplication against him.

Moses’ words call the calf the Samaritan’s god, indicating that he himself had adhered to its worship. Moses swears that it will be burned and scattered widely in the sea. Although some use “burn” to argue that the calf had been living flesh and blood, the phrase proves only that it was not pure gold. A more appropriate possibility is that la nuḥariqannahu refers to treating it as iron is cooled by a cooling apparatus, after which it would be scattered in the sea.
verses.98:
Al-Mizan takes this as Moses’ final address to the Samaritan and the Israelites, affirming that God alone is God and that neither the calf nor any imagined partner shares His divinity. In its context, the statement is subtle reasoning: because He alone is God, they can have no god besides Him.

The commentary rejects the claim that “He comprehends all things in (His) knowledge” proves that a non-existent may be called a thing. The verse says that everything called a thing is comprehended by God’s knowledge; it does not say that everything comprehended by His knowledge is called a thing, and only the latter claim would establish the proposed conclusion.
verses.99: Al-Mizan holds that the verse likely alludes to the distinctive character of Moses’ story: as that story was related, news of past affairs, events, and extinct nations will be related. The “Reminder” given by God is the Noble Qur’an, or the knowledge it contains through which He reminds people, including facts, stories, lessons, ethics, and laws.
verses.100: Al-Mizan explains that “it” refers to the Reminder. Although wizr can mean either burden or sin, “bearing” indicates a burden: whoever turns away from the Reminder will carry a burden of immense severity and bitter effect on the Day of Resurrection. Sin is metaphorically a burden because its bearer remains subject to it and carries it with difficulty.
verses.101: Al-Mizan explains abiding in the wizr as abiding in its jazāʾ, its punishment, by metonymy. The plural khālidīn follows the meaning of “whoever turns aside,” whereas the preceding singular verbs follow its wording. Read without this grammatical consideration, the two verses are among the clearest evidence that a person is punished only for his own deeds and abides in that punishment; this is the physical manifestation of deeds (tajassum al-aʿmāl). “Evil will it be” is an expression of disparagement: what an evil burden they will bear on the Day of Resurrection.
verses.102: Al-Mizan takes the blowing of the trumpet, placed in apposition to the Day of Resurrection, as an allusion to summoning and calling, as the later command to follow the inviter confirms. Zurq, “blue-eyed,” is best explained, following al-Farrāʾ, as blindness: when the light of the eyes departs, the iris turns blue. This is supported by the gathering of people blind on their faces on the Day of Resurrection. Explanations that make it bodily blueness from exhaustion and thirst, an allusion to Arabs’ dislike of blue eyes, or thirst altering the eyes’ blackness are judged unsatisfactory.
verses.103: Al-Mizan explains takhāfut as the low-voiced consultation of those assembled, caused by the scene’s horror. Their statement that they tarried only ten days means that, in comparison with the eternal abiding now confronting them, their prior earthly tarrying seems slight. The most truthful and fairest of them says it was only one day; this is closer to the truth, since limited earthly duration has no comparison with eternal abiding, though it remains only a relative, not literal, statement. The true account is that their tarrying lasted, by God’s ordinance, until the Day of Resurrection, as stated in (30:56).

The true account is that their tarrying lasted, by God’s ordinance, until the Day of Resurrection, as stated in (30:56).
verses.105: Al-Mizan explains that the people asked the Prophet about the mountains’ condition on the Day of Resurrection. God’s answer is that He will uproot and stir them up, leaving none in its place.
verses.106: Al-Mizan explains qāʾ as level ground and ṣafṣaf as smooth, level ground. After the mountains are removed, God will leave the earth an empty, smooth plain. The masculine pronoun is apparently used with regard to the mountains, though what is left is the earth.
verses.107: Al-Mizan explains ʿiwaj as sunken parts of the earth and amat as its raised parts. Though addressed to the Prophet, the statement concerns anyone who sees: no one will find the earth depressed like valleys or elevated like hills and hillocks.
verses.108:
Al-Mizan considers two possible links for “there is no crookedness in him.” If it qualifies the followers, they will have no choice but to follow the summons without hesitation, aversion, impediment, or indulgence, because the supposed independent power and ownership from which such resistance arises will then be seen to belong solely to God. If it qualifies the inviter, it means that he omits no one through inadvertence, forgetfulness, or overlooking. The following mention of voices lowered before the Beneficent better supports the first explanation, since raising one’s voice when summoned would express rebellion and disdain for obedience.

A hamas is a secret or extremely quiet sound, including the faint sound of feet. The address to the Prophet means every listener: people will be so absorbed in humbling and abasing themselves before God that only a low sound will be heard.
verses.109:
Al-Mizan explains the initial negation of effective intercession as affirming that just judgment, in accordance with the divine promise and threat, will certainly be carried out: no criminal’s transgression or sinner’s sin will be passed over through an impediment to judgment. The exception concerns permitted intercessors, rather than those for whom intercession is made. God’s leave is leave to intercede, since speech on that day depends on His permission.

“Whose word He is pleased with” is unrestricted, and therefore denotes speech wholly free from what angers God, whether intentional or inadvertent error. Such speech can only come from one whose heart God has purified from mistaken belief and misdeed and whose soul He has cleansed from polytheism and ignorance in this world, or from one joined with such people, since hearts will be tested and exposed on that day.
verses.110: Al-Mizan gives two possible referents for the plural pronouns. They may refer to those whom the Beneficent permits to intercede: God encompasses their pleasing words in knowledge, while they do not encompass Him and cannot deceive Him with embellished speech He does not approve. More fittingly in the context, they refer to the guilty. God knows their condition at the place of judgment, “before them,” and in the world before they arrive there, during life and after it, “behind them.” They are encompassed by His knowledge but cannot encompass Him; therefore He will punish their deeds, and, having submitted to the Ever-Living, Self-Subsistent, they cannot refuse His judgment, resulting in their disappointment.
verses.111:
Al-Mizan explains ʿanwah as submissiveness before the domination of the Dominator. When divine authority is manifest on the Day of Resurrection, every being other than God will be in this state: nothing truly owns anything, and all are absolutely poor and submissive. Humility is attributed to faces because it first appears in them; it also means that no impediment can prevent God’s judgment or decree. The names the Living and the Self-subsistent are especially apt because the dead are brought to life again and all causes are cut off from them, while God’s life and governance of every affair are absolute.

The failure of one who bears iniquity refers to unbelieving sinners, who receive the worst punishment. It does not include every sinful believer, for a believer will not be forsaken that day because of intercession. If the verse is read generally, each sinner’s failure is the loss of the particular happiness prevented by that iniquity, not necessarily the loss of happiness altogether.
verses.112:
Al-Mizan presents this as a digression explaining the pious believers, completing the contrast between them and sinners. Good works are conditioned by faith, because disbelief destroys works; hence the believing doer of good need fear neither injustice nor the withholding of what is due.

With this verse, the account of resurrection and requital is complete: people are summoned by the trumpet; their earthly tarrying appears negligible before eternal abiding; the earth is flattened for their gathering; they obediently follow the inviter; intercession cannot cancel punishment; God knows their state although they do not encompass Him in knowledge; they are humbled under His control and judgment; and the iniquitous undergo failure and punishment. This sequence explains the verses’ order and references.
verses.113:
Al-Mizan explains “thus” as referring to the detailed manner of explanation in the preceding verses. God sent down the Book as an Arabic Qur’an and varied the presentation of some of His threats, bringing them in one form after another, so that people might guard against evil or receive a reminder.

Here ittiqāʾ does not mean the taqwā arising from faith, namely obedience and avoidance of disobedience. Rather, in contrast with remembrance, it means refraining from enmity and obstinacy toward the truth out of fear that the threatened harm may be real. The reminder is the realization of remembrance and awareness of the truth, leading them to believe in it. God knows best.
verses.114:
Al-Mizan takes the glorification of God as consequent primarily on the preceding discussion of resurrection and requital, together with the Qur’an’s threats and guidance. God is the King who disposes absolutely within His kingdom: He sends messengers and Books to guide people, resurrects and summons them, and recompenses their good and evil deeds as they stand humbled before the Ever-Living, Self-Subsistent. He is King at the beginning and the end, and the Truth, established and unchanging. The glorification may also conclude everything from Moses’ story onward.

The prohibition against hastening with the Qur’an concerns the Prophet’s reception and recitation of revelation. He would hasten to recite what was being revealed before the Angel of revelation had completed it; he was commanded instead to wait until its revelation ended. The command to ask, “O my Lord! increase me in knowledge,” replaces premature recitation: rather than act on a vague prior knowledge of what remains unrevealed, he should patiently seek fresh knowledge from God and listen to the rest of the revelation.

Al-Mizan holds that this supports oral traditions that the Qur’an was revealed altogether, not in portions, since hurrying to recite what had not yet been revealed would otherwise make no sense. It rejects two proposed readings as incompatible with the verse’s wording: that the Prophet was forbidden to recite or dictate the Qur’an to his Companions before its meanings were explained, and that he was forbidden to request further Qur’anic revelation before the current revelation was complete.
verses.115: Al-Mizan explains that the covenant (ʿahd) made with Adam was advice, namely the prohibition against approaching the tree. Nisyān may mean literal forgetting, but may also metonymically mean failing to do what was enjoined, since what is forgotten is left undone. ʿAzm is firm resolve to act and can also mean forbearance, because it requires resolute determination. Thus the verse means that Adam forsook the divine advice and was not found to have the resolve, or forbearance, to uphold it.
verses.116:
Al-Mizan takes the account of the angels’ obeisance as joined to an implied command to recall God’s covenant with Adam, so that Adam’s failure to keep it may be understood. Iblīs’ refusal answers the implicit question of what he did when the angels were commanded to prostrate. God’s consequent warning that Iblīs was Adam’s and his wife’s enemy was advisory direction toward their good.

The command, “therefore let him not drive you both forth from the Garden,” is addressed to Adam in the form of reference to Iblīs: it means that Adam must neither obey Iblīs nor neglect his trickery and insinuation, lest Iblīs gain mastery over them and cause their expulsion. Al-Mizan dismisses the various reasons reported by Imam al-Rāzī for Iblīs’ enmity. Its real basis was God’s preferring and honoring the human species over Iblīs, followed by his expulsion, damnation, and curse; commanding obeisance to Adam likewise signified obeisance to mankind.

The resulting shaqāʾ is drudgery: outside the Garden, human beings must labor amid worldly needs for food, drink, clothing, and shelter. The following descriptions of freedom from hunger, nakedness, thirst, and heat establish this meaning. They also show that the prohibition was advisory rather than authoritative: its violation naturally brought the hardship consequent upon leaving the Garden, not a religious transgression punishable in the Hereafter. The covenant also preceded the legislation of religion, which began only with the command to leave the Garden and descend to the earth.

The singular in fatashqā, “you should be unhappy,” is because the covenant and address concern Adam; the surrounding references to forgetting, resolve, hunger, clothing, thirst, heat, Satan’s suggestion, Adam’s disobedience, and God’s choosing him are likewise singular. The dual is used only where both Adam and his wife must be included. Al-Mizan rejects the claim that the singular assigns Adam alone the burden of maintaining woman, since the subsequent assurances would then have been expressed in the dual.

verses.118: Al-Mizan explains that ḍaḥw denotes the sun striking or shining upon someone. Freedom from it means that the sun’s heat has no effect requiring shelter from heat or cold. The verse’s four privations are arranged rhetorically to preserve the pauses; their underlying sequence is freedom from hunger, thirst, nakedness, and exposure to the sun.
verses.119: Al-Mizan explains that ḍaḥw denotes the sun striking or shining upon someone. Freedom from it means that the sun’s heat has no effect requiring shelter from heat or cold. The verse’s four privations are arranged rhetorically to preserve the pauses; their underlying sequence is freedom from hunger, thirst, nakedness, and exposure to the sun.
verses.120:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Shaytan, the evil one, is Iblīs’ name on account of his evil. The “tree of immortality” is the forbidden tree, whose fruit Satan represented as conferring everlasting life; “a kingdom which decays not (lā yablā)” means a rule untouched by time, rivals, and impediments. Thus Satan offered Adam everlasting life together with an enduring kingdom, and lā yablā is not merely emphatic repetition.

There is no contradiction between this verse’s conjunction of immortality and imperishable kingdom and Sūrah al-Aʿrāf’s presentation of the matter as alternatives. The alternative formulation may deny that neither attribute applies, rather than deny that both apply; it concerns the object of the prohibition, while this verse affirms that the tree was represented as having both attributes.
verses.121:
Al-Mizan refers the explanation of Adam and his wife covering themselves with Garden leaves to Sūrah al-Aʿrāf. It explains al-ghayy not as ḍalāl, straying from the path, but as the opposite of al-rushd: failing to hit upon what is right. Hudā is opposed to both terms, but means guidance in one sense when opposed to error and showing or conveying someone along a path when opposed to ḍalāl.

Adam’s disobedience was of an advisory instruction, not an authoritative command. Prophets are protected from sin and transgression in receiving, preserving, and conveying revealed religion, whether through speech or conduct; their deeds cannot contradict their divinely communicated words. But compliance with a sincere counselor’s advisory instruction, which directs one to life’s benefits and the better course, does not concern the proofs of prophetic infallibility. This may be what is intended by the claim that, despite infallibility, prophets may leave what is best (tark al-awlā), as Adam did by eating from the tree. Competing exegeses of the verse reflect their schools’ differing positions on prophetic infallibility.
verses.122:
Al-Mizan explains ijtibāʾ as gathering by way of selection, including God’s gathering a servant exclusively for Himself and making him one of the mukhlaṣīn (the most sincere). Accordingly, after choosing Adam, God turned to him, guided him, and advanced him toward Himself, as though gathering his scattered parts into unity.

Although hadā is unqualified, the context of divine choosing indicates guidance to God Himself, the root of every guidance. It is nevertheless restricted to religion—true belief and good deeds—because it follows upon Adam’s being chosen. Al-Mizan therefore rejects the objection that the guidance, following Adam’s ghiwāyah in an advisory matter, must signify comprehensive protection from error in both authoritative and advisory matters, religious and secular. The guidance belongs to the purpose for which he was chosen: religious happiness through servitude to God.

This guidance reaches the servant directly, without intervening causes or delay. Guidance to worldly benefits, though also from God, operates through causes that may fail.
verses.123:
Al-Mizan holds that the shift in “He said: Get forth you two” may serve to emphasize that the judgment and decree stated in the verse belong exclusively to God. The coming of guidance after the descent is a judgment consequent upon the fall. Its emphatic wording establishes that divine guidance will inevitably come.

“To follow My guidance” is metonymical for following the guide who guides by God’s guidance. Whoever does so will neither stray on the path nor be unhappy at its destination and final outcome. Since neither ḍalāl nor shaqāʾ is qualified, both are negated in this world and the Hereafter.

God’s guidance is what He calls people to through His prophets. It conforms to the innate human nature (fiṭra) and consists of beliefs and deeds to which human instinct and disposition call in accordance with humanity’s given constitution. Every being’s happiness lies in what its disposition and equipment require; no happiness lies beyond this.
verses.124:
Al-Mizan explains that “whoever turns away from My reminder” contrasts with following God’s guidance, but states the cause of the ruling: neglecting God and turning from His reminder cause both a wretched life and resurrection in blindness. “Reminder” may mean remembering God, the Qur’an or all divine books, or the call of truth, which necessarily entails remembrance of God.

A “straitened life” is a wretched, constricted life. One who forgets his Lord is left clinging to the world as his sole pursuit. Whether his livelihood is small or abundant, it never satisfies him; he continually seeks more and suffers constriction of heart, anxiety, grief, fear, disappointment, loss, illness, and other calamities. By contrast, one who knows and remembers his Lord knows that the world is transient beside the Hereafter and is satisfied with his allotted provision, even if it is only the bare minimum.

Al-Mizan rejects limiting the phrase to punishment of the grave merely because some who turn from God possess abundant worldly means. The Qur’an does not judge wealth and poverty in themselves, but distinguishes the contented believer who remembers God from the one attached to worldly life and dissatisfied with all he has. Punishment of the grave may be an instance of the straitened life, since barzakh follows worldly life. It also rejects interpreting the phrase exclusively as the constriction of Hell on the Day of Resurrection, because the first clause is unqualified while resurrection is specifically qualified; that reading is valid only if the first clause is taken generally to include life in both worlds.

Being raised blind means not being guided to the place of happiness, namely Paradise.
verses.125:
Al-Mizan notes that the question about having been seeing in the world initially suggests blindness in the physical sense. This appears to conflict with verses depicting the guilty as seeing the terrors and signs of the Resurrection. Some therefore say that they will be raised seeing and later blinded, or will alternate between sight and blindness.

The commentary rejects this as an analogy between the Hereafter and the natural order of this world. The Qur’an and Sunnah establish that the Hereafter has a different governing order. There is no reason that blindness there must mean inability to see everything visible. The guilty may be unable to see the way to happiness, success, victory, and honored life, while still seeing the evidence completing the case against them, the terrors of Resurrection, Hellfire, and what intensifies their punishment.
verses.126:
Al-Mizan explains the reply as reciprocal requital: just as the guilty person is raised blind, God’s communications came to him and he neglected them; and just as he neglected those communications, God forsakes him on the Day of Resurrection. His blindness is being left to himself without guidance to salvation, corresponding to his failure in the world to be guided by God’s communications.

God calls both the guilty person’s turning from His remembrance and forsaking His guidance, and God’s punishment of blindness and forsaking him, nisyān. The conclusion thus returns to Adam’s forgetting of the covenant. Adam’s Garden story is presented as an earlier parable of what will happen to his descendants until the Day of Resurrection: the prohibition of the tree resembles the later religious call and divine guidance, while Adam’s neglect of the covenant resembles his descendants’ neglect of God’s remembrance and communications. The difference is that Adam’s test preceded the legislation of Shariah; its prohibition was advisory, and his act was leaving what was preferred, unlike his descendants’ disobedience.
verses.127: Al-Mizan explains isrāf as exceeding the proper limit. “And thus” apparently resumes the previously mentioned punishment of one who turns from God’s remembrance and forgets His communications: this is a transgression against the bounds of servitude and a rejection of communications made a covenant with him. The punishment therefore belongs to one who forsakes God’s communications and His remembrance. The chastisement of the Hereafter is more severe and lasting than worldly chastisement because it encompasses both the inward and outward person and never ceases.
verses.128: Al-Mizan takes yahdi, “direct,” as including the sense of making clear: if they believe in God’s communications and seek instruction, should it not be evident that many earlier generations were destroyed while their dwelling places remained on routes travelled by the people of Mecca? Their journeys passed the habitations of ʿĀd in Yemen, Thamūd and the dwellers of the thicket in Syria, and Lot’s people in Palestine. These are signs for uli al-Nuha, those endowed with understanding.
verses.129:
Al-Mizan holds that lizām, as required by the context, means mulazamah, “inseparability”: had not a prior word from God and an appointed term intervened, destruction would have become inseparable from these people as soon as they exceeded the limits and disbelieved in their Lord’s communications. The alternatives that take lizām as an instrument-noun or as the plural of lāzim do not fit the context well.

The prior word is the judgment given when Adam descended to the earth, under which humanity has an abode and provision on earth for a fixed time. Thus people are protected from exterminatory punishment for extravagance and unbelief until their appointed term, unless a Messenger comes and decides between them: “And every nation had a Messenger; so when their Messenger came, the matter was decided between them with justice and they shall not be dealt with unjustly” (10:47). This also covers a people who request a sign and then disbelieve after it comes. This community likewise enjoys protection through that prior promise, while judgment between it and the Prophet has been deferred to another time.

The commentary rejects the view that the word is a promise exclusive to this community to postpone punishment until the Resurrection, since the literal sense of the relevant verses conflicts with it, though they do indicate postponement to another time. It also rejects the claim that the word refers to the decision to kill those at Badr by the sword and that the appointed term concerns the remaining Meccan unbelievers. The appointed term is the fixed time that cannot be advanced or deferred: “No people can hasten on their doom nor can they postpone (it)” (15:5). Neither identifying it simply with the Day of Resurrection nor treating it as merely explanatory of the prior word has evidence.

Accordingly, the prior word and the appointed term together constitute one complete reason for delaying punishment, not two independent reasons. The address, “your Lord,” also reinforces and supports the Prophet.
verses.130:
Al-Mizan connects the command to patience with the preceding postponement of the opponents’ punishment. Since God has decided not to hasten vengeance for what they say, the Prophet is to endure it, accept God’s decision, declare God free from their polytheism and from the evil they inflict, and praise Him for the effects of His decree. Such evils belong to their agents and are evil in themselves, so God is absolved of them; yet through His permission they are connected to Him and become beautiful through the general benefits by which the order of the universe is maintained. For this, He is glorified and praised.

The commands concern glorification before sunrise, before sunset, at some times of night, and wa aṭrāf al-nahār. Tasbīḥ is unqualified in the wording, which does not itself establish that it means the obligatory prayers. Most exegetes nevertheless identify it with prayer, following reports from early authorities such as Qatādah. They consequently read the verse as prescribing the five prayers: dawn before sunrise, late afternoon before sunset, sunset and evening in the night, and noon in “the edges of the day.” They explain noon as an edge of each half of a day divided at midday, and explain the plural aṭrāf either as usable for two or by taking “day” generically. Al-Mizan finds this basis far from sound: the middle of the day cannot naturally be called the edges of the day through such contrived considerations.

Others take tasbīḥ as unrestricted inward or verbal glorification and praise, such as subḥānallāh (glory be to God) and al-ḥamdu lillāh (praise be to God). They identify the edges with dawn and late afternoon, sometimes adding midday, and explain the plural as dual usage and the repetition as emphasis. The commentary judges that the same essential difficulty remains: the applicability of aṭrāf al-nahār to midday or to dawn and late afternoon.

Its own proposal is that wa aṭrāf al-nahār is an accompanying object (mafʿūl maʿahu), not a further time qualifier. The “edges of the day” are the extended periods before sunrise and before sunset; each contains parts that are edges relative to the day’s middle, so they may be called aṭrāf as well as ṭarafay. The meaning is therefore to glorify before sunrise and sunset—which are the day’s edges—and at some times of night along with those edges. Min in “during hours of the night” supplies the temporal sense there; aṭrāf al-nahār means accompaniment, while the temporal qualification is understood on both sides. This removes both the supposed repetition and the need to use a plural for fewer than three.

If tasbīḥ means unrestricted glorification, the command concerns parts of the beginning and end of the day and parts of the night. If it means the obligatory prayers, it specifies only dawn, late afternoon, sunset, and evening prayer, as in: “And keep up prayer in the two parts of the day and in the first hours of the night” (11:114). Calling the two daytime periods aṭrāf may indicate their extended duration. There is no difficulty in the verse containing four rather than five prayers: Sūrah Ṭā Hā was among the early Meccan revelations, while exhaustive Sunni and Shiʿa traditions place the prescription of five daily prayers at the Ascension, after which came: “Keep up prayer from the declining of the sun till the darkness of the night and the morning recitation” (17:78). It may be that four prayers had then been prescribed and noon prayer had not.

“That you may be well pleased” means that, through patience and persistent glorification and praise, the Prophet may become content with God’s decree and assignment. Repeatedly declaring God’s action free from defect and praising its beauty comforts the soul, removes distorted perceptions, and fixes in it the recognition that it loves what is beautiful and free from ugliness. Thus constant remembrance produces contentment with the decree. It is also said that the phrase means intercession and an exalted station before God, or the promised worldly help and strengthening of religion together with intercession and Paradise in the Hereafter.
verses.131:
Al-Mizan explains “stretching the eye” as prolonging one’s gaze, a metaphor for attachment to and love of what is seen. Azwāj may mean different classes of unbelievers or their male-and-female households; its indefiniteness belittles them and indicates that they deserve no attention. The “splendor of this world’s life” explicates what they have been given: its adornment and enjoyment.

Fitnah means trial or test; alternatively, it is said to mean punishment, since abundance of wealth and children may itself be God’s chastisement of them. In contrast, the sustenance given by the Lord means the sustenance of the Hereafter, which is better and more enduring. The verse thus forbids attachment to the worldly embellishment granted to some of them as a test, directing attention instead to the superior and abiding provision of the Hereafter.
verses.132:
Al-Mizan regards the verse as Meccan, in keeping with the chapter’s overall thread and in the absence of any claim that it is an exception. At the time of its revelation, ahlak therefore means Khadījah, the Prophet’s wife, and ʿAlī, his family member who lived in his house; it may also include some of his daughters. Interpretations extending it, in its original setting, to all his wives, daughters, and ʿAlī; to Banū Hāshim and Banū al-Muṭṭalib; or to the entire community are incorrect. The first extension may be valid for the verse’s continuing applicability, but not for its circumstances of revelation, since in Mecca the Prophet had no wife besides Khadījah.

“We ask you no provision; We provide you” means that God has no need of them, whereas they are needy and dependent upon Him. It does not charge the Prophet with providing for creatures or for himself. The good end belongs to guarding against evil, just as God accepts the guarding against evil of those who offer sacrifice, not their flesh or blood.

The restriction to commanding his family to pray, together with the preceding instructions to the Prophet alone concerning four prayers, patience, and indifference to the unbelievers’ provision, suggests that the chapter, or this verse in particular, was revealed near the beginning of the Prophetic mission. Ibn Masʿūd is reported to have called Sūrah Ṭā Hā one of the very early first sūrahs (al-ʿitāq al-uwal).
verses.133:
Al-Mizan identifies these words as those of the Meccan polytheists, who disparaged the Qur’an as not being a sign of prophethood and demanded another miracle like those given to earlier peoples. Their demand is goading intended to insult the Qur’an and portray the Prophet as powerless.

The response, “Has not there come to them a clear evidence of what is in the previous books?”, has two possible readings of bayyinah. If it means a clear proof, the Qur’an itself confirms and explains the true knowledge and religious laws contained in the Torah, the Gospels, and the other heavenly scriptures, though it was brought by one not taught or dictated to by a human teacher. If it means an explanation, it recounts what the earlier books tell of communities that demanded miraculous signs, received them, and were destroyed when they then disbelieved. They should therefore refrain from demanding a sign beyond the Qur’an.
verses.134:
Al-Mizan considers it likely that min qablihi, “before this,” refers in meaning to the clear proof of the preceding verse, namely the Qur’an, though the pronoun is masculine because the Qur’an is masculine. Had God destroyed them for their extravagance and unbelief before the proof reached them, the case against them would not have been complete and they could have protested that no Messenger had been sent, through whom they would have followed God’s communications before suffering disgrace and shame.

It is also said that the pronoun literally refers to the Prophet inferred from the preceding context. This better suits the outward wording, especially their demand for a Messenger, but the first interpretation better suits the intended meaning. Their words support it, since they say that they would have followed God’s communications, not merely that they would have followed His Messenger.
verses.135:
Al-Mizan explains tarabbuṣ as waiting and al-ṣirāt al-sawiyy as the even path. “Every one is awaiting” means that both sides wait: the believers await God’s promise concerning the opponents, the advancement of His religion, and the completion of His light, while the opponents hope for calamity to defeat the true call. Each pursues a path to its goal; therefore they are told to wait.

The statement is a threat: they will learn which party follows the straight path that reaches its destination and which is rightly guided to that destination. It alludes to the great battle and gives tidings of victory.
